utterances.text: And how must -- how can the Chamber decide on -- is that then tendering from the bar table, which introduces a new element, that is that the words of Mr. Seselj were recorded -- I do not know whether any other persons do appear on the -- or is it all one big interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is all one big interview that was a sit-down interview by the BBC of Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The date, which has been indicated previously, was March 1995. Now, with respect to the exhibit, we are tendering the entire interview as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is how long approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately an hour and 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour and 40 minutes, which means we have seen approximately 5 per cent of what we're supposed to -- I'm not saying that it's -- couldn't be done, but I'm just trying to define in what situation we find ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I may. As Your Honour noted right at the outset when I asked these questions and tendered, we'd be happy to agree to these things and have them admitted; however, in the absence of agreement, we do have to spend time in court and present the exhibits to a witness who can actually authenticate and identify who the person is that is speaking in the video. That is the reason this was presented to the witness. We are offering it for its full content. We submit this is admissible. It's relevant. It's relevant, the clips that were played, with respect to this particular witness's testimony that is already noted by Defence. There is a nexus between this witness and Mr. Seselj. He has explained his history of personally meeting Mr. Seselj and recognising his voice. He was clear and unambiguous of his recognition of Mr. Seselj. This is an unedited interview by a charged co-perpetrator of the joint criminal enterprise. We submit that it's relevant, and we would seek to enter the entire video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's unedited. How do you know, from what appears, that it's unedited?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's -- it's a continuous video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not the same as unedited, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when it's the Prosecution's intention just to have confirmation that this is Mr. Seselj and his voice, why then tender one hour and a half of the same material?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what Mr. Weber tells us. Mr. Weber tells us that we showed this video to this witness because his testimony is related to events Mr. Seselj is talking about as well, and apart from that, this witness is able to recognise the face and the voice of Mr. Seselj. Now, there are three levels: Who is this who speaks? Do we know who it is? Second is: What does he say? And third is: What is the relation between what he said and what other people say or what we learn from other evidence? I do understand that if Mr. Weber says that he tenders this video for its content that he specifically refers to level 1 and level 2, that is: Who's speaking? And second: What is he saying? And that the third level, whether there's any relation between what Mr. Seselj says, whether he's reading a fairytale or whether he's telling us things which have a relation with evidence this Chamber will hear, that's still open, I take it, Mr. Weber, and I take it that, at the end of the case, that you would like to draw our attention to the -- to the links between what is said in this video and what happened on the ground as told to us by other evidence or by other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct. And ultimately the Prosecution -- it's for the Chamber to decide the weight to be attributed to this piece of evidence with respect to that third factor which has just been noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One additional question: Mr. Jovanovic, you said we should know whether it's broadcasted. Now, whether a video is broadcasted seems to be relevant if you want to establish that the public had an opportunity to view it. When I'm talking about the three levels, the first level being: Who is it? Do you recognise his face? Do you recognise his voice? Is -- therefore, it's irrelevant for this broadcast. Second level: What is this person saying? Also whether it's broadcasted or not is unrelated to what the person says. Even if you put it on the shelf and never broadcast it, these, nevertheless, are the words apparently recorded of things he said. For this third level: The link between what happened and what we learn from other evidence, it may or may be irrelevant whether it was broadcasted or not. Broadcasting appears to be specifically relevant if you want to establish that not only the person who made the video and not only the person who spoke on this video, but that the public in more general terms could have known about it because it was broadcasted. I'd like to very clearly always identify what we are talking about, and I have not heard anything in relation to this BBC clips what the relevance of it being broadcasted is. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My objection was about the showing of the first video-clip. I only said that we should have complete data about a video-clip, when it was made, who made it, and whether it was ever broadcast; however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, if you're talking about the first clip, we have two 65 ter numbers, the first being 1932, which is the one assembled by B-92; and we have the second series consisting of three clips, being the BBC, that's 65 ter 2853. Now, your objection, as far as broadcasting is concerned, did it relate to the three BBC clips or did it relate to the two until-now played B-92 clips? Because at this moment, we're only discussing admission into evidence of the three BBC clips. So I'm asking you what the relevance of this being broadcasted or not being broadcasted would be for admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this refers to the BBC interview lasting one hour and 45 minutes. As far as I understood my learned friends from the Prosecution, they want the whole recording admitted. That interview by Vojislav Seselj encompasses his interpretation, or rather, he spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, my simple question was: What the relevance is of this BBC video being broadcasted, yes or no, for the admission into evidence? I'm not asking about whether what Mr. Seselj said is true or not true, personal views -- that was not my question to you. My question was relevance of this being broadcasted or not being broadcasted for our decision to admit into evidence this BBC video which -- of which three small portions were played and of which the Prosecution seeks to be admitted into evidence, the whole of it close to two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. There may have been a misunderstanding. I did not object to the BBC clip, i.e., I did not say anything about the interview being broadcast or not. My objection with regard to the BBC interview is this: Vojislav Seselj, who the witness identified, is heard talking about many other things apart from those that the witness is testifying about, which is Slavonia and the events in Borovo Selo. For example, Vojislav Seselj also mentions events in Zvornik, and this particular witness has nothing whatsoever to do or had nothing whatsoever to do with those particular events. There may have been a misunderstanding with regard to the fact whether the BBC interview was ever broadcast or not, and I apologise if I have been the cause of the misunderstanding. What I'm saying is that the interview, lasting one hour and 45 minutes, depicts Vojislav Seselj talking about many other things and locations that are not connected with the testimony of this witness, which would rule out the video-clip as material for admission, except for the part talking about the events in Borovo Selo. That's why I am objecting to the whole interview being admitted evidence and I'm not objecting to the three video-clips, shown earlier today in the courtroom, being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Final question to both Defence teams, and the Chamber will take its time to decide on the matter. Last question: If this would have been tendered - and to some extent, of course, it is tendered from the bar table - just to say these were the views Mr. Seselj expressed at the time when this video was -- when this interview was held, so as to consider this together with all the other evidence to see what the probative value of it is. What would be your position? Because to some extent, this BBC - and that's not the same with the B-92 - is to a greater extent tendered from the bar table. That is, this is what was said at the time by Mr. Seselj which has some relevance in the context of the matters this Chamber has to decide upon. Would that -- what would be the objections? Because 95 per cent of it is tendered from the bar table. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Your Honours has formulated it, we would have no objection to the tendering of these three portions. But we still maintain our objection that when it contains words of the person on the clip saying, I heard from that person some information, in our view it would not be permissible or admissible in terms of double hearsay. These are objections to the form of hearsay would still stand. But in principle -- and Mr. Seselj gives his views on a certain situation, of course, we would not object to the tendering of that information. Of course, not when the witness can identify the name and the voice of that particular person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So a portion of our primary objection would remain, namely, the double hearsay standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the double hearsay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as such remains, whereas even the whole of the video being tendered from the bar table does not meet any objections, but you would say that if there's any double hearsay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- elsewhere in this video, then we would, for the same reasons, exclude those portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, I also concur with my learned friend, Mr. Jovanovic, that the clips should only be admitted as shown in court and not insofar as the remaining of the one hour, 45 minutes contains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there of course is an issue. If I say "tendered from the bar table," I mean to say that you put an exhibit before the Chamber even if a witness has not testified about it as a contemporaneous or contemporaneously-created document or video so as to consider it on the basis of its content. That could be a document, that could be a series of documents. So I have some difficulties in understanding how you say that you would not oppose against tendering it from the bar table, whereas the -- I would say the specific element in tendering from the bar table is that it has not been shown in full. It's just made available to the Chamber on the basis of the content itself, in this case, a video showing Mr. Seselj, where Mr. Seselj says all kind of things. We will later have to decide whether what he says is personal opinion, is true, is in any relation with the events on the ground. We'll have to find out what it actually is, and that's what we call evaluation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it may assist the Chamber, in paragraph 23 of the Perisic guide-lines the Court addresses the tendering of evidence from the bar table, and the situation what they refer to bulky exhibits or exhibits with bulky portions is addressed, saying that: "The tendering party should file a table containing a short description of each exhibit, as well as its relevance and probative value if not immediately obvious from the description. In case of bulky exhibits ..." And I think we can draw the analogy with bulky video-clips, with particular relevant portions, a reference to those portions is needed. So I take from this decision that it's not an automatic mechanism that in terms of tendering evidence from the bar table the Court has to accept full video-clip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we do not have to accept. There's no question about that, Mr. Knoops. What I'm talking about is whether there are obstacles to admission, and now -- but it's a new argument you're raising now. You say it's bulk material, which is -- first of all, these are guide-lines in one case, and apparently is more about admissibility policy rather than admissibility as legal standard. But I do understand you say this material is too bulky to be admitted in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I hope you see the consequence. If this conduct of the Prosecution should be allowed, the Defence is forced to cross-examine every witness on the contents of video-clip of one hour, 45 minutes, although it has no relevance to the case or there is no relationship with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that is the consequence depends on what you want to establish in cross-examination. Until now, we have nothing more than in examination-in-chief that the Prosecution says: We want to put before the Chamber this piece of evidence in which the Chamber can see what the position was at the time as expressed by Mr. Seselj. There's nothing more, there's nothing less. If you want to cross-examine the witness on that -- then, of course, we'll follow your cross-examination, and we'll finally find out whether it assists the Chamber in its work. But I see your last argument was it's too bulky and will take up too much time in cross-examination. Mr. Jovanovic, anything further to add, and specifically in relation to my question to have this admitted as being tendered from the bar table. That goes beyond the portions played and only about the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is the intention of the OTP to tender the entire video footage from the bar table, then we need, I think, additional information as to what the video footage contains in relation to the places which are of relevance to this case and which Mr. Seselj also mentions in his speech. So more information is required on that in order for this exhibit to be admitted from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, is there anything you'd like to add? I'm not encouraging you to spend much more time on it, but since all the objections, I think it's fair that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would prefer not to spend this much court time on matters such as this. If it would be possible to agree to these things, we would. We -- there's no apparent objection to the authenticity of this video at the time, that it is Mr. Seselj throughout the video. With respect to the bulkiness of this exhibit -- the transcript's only 42 pages. There's much more voluminous material that comes before this Chamber on a daily basis. The volume of material that is provided to the parties is of much greater volume. This is not bulky or voluminous material. Furthermore, this was provided to the Defence on April 25th, 2008. They have had this entire 42 pages of this interview for an extraordinarily long period of time, to review it and be familiar with it. This witness has particular knowledge about the clips, those that were shown to him. To avoid having to repeatedly have the same conversation with every witness that comes and to establish particular relevance of each clip, would not be in the interests of judicial economy. It's clear who it is. Mr. Jovanovic very pertinently pointed out there is discussion of Zvornik. That is also relevant to this case. Now, is the Prosecution, when the video is clearly Mr. Seselj throughout with every witness, supposed to show the video -- that portion to the witness just to merely establish, again, that it's Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not needed because the parties agree that it's Mr. Seselj, unless the parties make a difference and want to say that Mr. Seselj is in the first minute but not in the 10th minute or not at the 20th minute. So that is agreed upon so that will cause us no problems. Any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, the Chamber will consider the matter but will first take a break. We'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, that's how lawyers operate in courtrooms. For the parties, the Chamber has considered the matter. The whole of the video will be marked for identification. The Prosecution is invited to consider whether we really need the whole of the two hours in terms of relevance, importance, probative value. At the same time, the parties, Prosecution and Defence, are urged to see whether they can reach any agreement on a reduced portion to be tendered. The Defence, of course, is aware of the context of the whole of it. At the same time, the Chamber or at least members of the Chamber will read the transcript overnight. I already can tell the parties that, as I said before, that this is not material which is inadmissible, but whether we'll admit anything more than the three portions, we'll first have a look at the whole of it and again, you're invited to see whether you can reduce; you're invited to see whether you can agree on the matter. And if we are informed about an agreement, we'll consider that agreement; if there's no agreement, the Chamber will decide. That's -- and for the time being, the whole of the video, almost two hours, will be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the 65 ter 2853 of which three smaller portions were played, BBC interview with Mr. Vojislav Seselj would receive ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit P18, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet with Goran Hadzic on the 7th or 8th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: On the left bank of the Danube, on the other side from Borovo Selo where there was a ferry, a ferry crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was anyone else present with Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: As I know, all -- as I do not know all of the people, there was a new face that I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to have a conversation with Mr. Hadzic about this new person?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him who that was and he said, That is my body-guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you later learn who this body-guard was?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: After that I went to the office of the mayor of Backa Palanka, Ljubo Novakovic and I asked him who Goran Hadzic's body-guard was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Novakovic tell you?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: He told me that he was from the DB, and that his name was Lazar Sarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "DB," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were expressions that were used. I was referring to the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you also then, after this initial meeting, have occasion to personally interact with the person who you learned to be Lazar Sarac?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after a while I met with Lazar Sarac, and it turned out that he knew me better than I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During the course of these meetings, did -- was the name of Lazar Sarac confirmed to you by Lazar Sarac himself?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes, and also that he worked for the DB. That was no secret at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with someone in the spring of 1992 in relation to the subject of unification of agricultural property?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I was aware of this initiative to amalgamate all the farming land in this stretch from Sid to Vukovar or better to put it from Tovarnik to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was this individual that you had a conversation with?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: I just had a chance meeting in Sid with Slobodan Medic, who already then was leading a formation known as Skorpioni. They were stationed at Djeletovci to protect the oilfield, at least that is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: At his invitation for a drink, he said that he had something to tell me, and he started telling me how he had been to see the boss the day before and that they had talked about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you respond to this information?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: I asked him, Who is your boss? And he answered, Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I think you've referenced this in part, but who is Slobodan Medic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Medic set up a unit which had for its objective the protection of the oilfields at Djeletovci, they said, and at the same time they pursued these other jobs. But at any rate they were armed, they were uniformed, and they were equipped as a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was the name of this unit?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Skorpioni. They had a patch on their overalls, an emblem of the scorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The reason the Prosecution requested to continue the proceedings in private session is because the next exhibit is subject to a currently pending Rule 54 bis application by the Republic of Serbia. The Prosecution maintains that this exhibit should not be placed under seal and the related testimony should be public; however, due to this pending motion, we requested the discussion related to this today be held in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection to dealing with the matter in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection with this caveat, but we're not sure which exhibit we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but then that will appear from the next question, I take it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash is correct. Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of 65 ter 4822.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the exhibit before you?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this document and let the Court know if you are personally familiar with the subject of this exhibit. If you need to see a different portion or need to continue reading, if you could please let us know.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: From a conversation with Mr. Medic and otherwise. There was an intention for the complete arable land to be merged and placed under control, and this was to a view of controlling the overall production.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the information in this DB report consistent with your conversation with Slobodan Medic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could page 3 of the B/C/S version of the exhibit please be placed on the screen. If we could please have it remain on the same page of the English version, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to the fifth line from the top, this is in the second paragraph of the English version in italics, does this exhibit discuss the consolidation of a particular agricultural plant to which you were employed?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since all the arable land, or maybe 90 per cent of it between Tovarnik and Vukovar, was land that my combine was in charge of and worked on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the name of the company that is referred to, to which you were formerly employed?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Vupik Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the English version and page 4 of the B/C/S version of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, what is the name of the operative on this report?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Lazar Sarac is the operative in question and the signature is his.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tender 65 ter 4822 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be exhibit number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P19, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P19 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please return to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into open session. The exhibit just admitted in private session is admitted under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention back to May 1991, did you have occasion to go to the Serbian parliament in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you make this trip?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, 1991, upon the invitation of the speaker of the parliament, Pavic Obradovic, that's when I went for the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting when you arrived in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the parliament of the Republic of Serbia. According to my estimate, it was the group of MPs of the Socialist Party of Serbia, that's who -- that is who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please provide us with the names.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Pavic Obradovic, Boro Petrovic, both vice-presidents; and I believe that the president of the legislation committee, Radmilo Bogdanovic, was there; or Bojovic was also there, also an MP; Bato Zivanovic was there; and also some others who I didn't know, or at least I didn't know their names, but I know they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was the reason you were called to Belgrade for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: The reason was the liquidation or assassination of Soskocanin, Vukasin on that same day at 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe the -- it's correct on the transcript. After this meeting did you have occasion to speak with anyone?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the meeting, we went to Mr. Obradovic's office. I, myself; Radmilo Bogdanovic himself; and three or four other men whose names I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was discussed when you met with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting which proceeded, I expressed my dissatisfaction with the whole situation, and I offered some solutions that might have helped us, and I'm referring to the territory of Slavonia. And then in the office, Radmilo Bogdanovic and I were involved in the discussion that everybody else only listened to. I simply asked him why he kept on sending us thieves and criminals to our neck of the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did Mr. Bogdanovic respond to this?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: He said this, Don't you think that some day I will be taken to task for what I'm doing today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was said after that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: He saw that I was excited or at least thought I was. He tried to calm me down, and then he said to me, We gave you Arkan as commander, we gave you Martic as the head of police, talk to them and try to deal with the problems that you're facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you said that they were sending you criminals and thieves, who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: People who were being sent to us, but at that particular moment when he mentioned Arkan, I said, No criminal will ever be my commander. And I will stay here in Belgrade. And as for you, you can go over there together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "him," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to Arkan. What I meant was if you're sending Arkan over there as my commander, then you may as well join him. I, myself, don't need a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After your conversation with Radmilo Bogdanovic on the 15th of May, 1991, did you meet Arkan while in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry, where did this meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: In a cafe called Trozubac in Nusiceva Street across the street from the Matica Iseljenika, which was an NGO headed by Brana Crncevic, and I was involved in the work of that NGO in terms of looking after and assisting refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many days after your conversation on the 15th of May with Mr. Bogdanovic did this meeting with Arkan occur?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: On the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was said between you and Arkan when you met in the Trozubac cafe?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: An acquaintance of mine took me there, saying, A friend of mine wants to meet you. I entered the cafe, and Arkan was sitting there in a corner. We greeted each other. That was our first encounter. At the very beginning me said to me, For everybody else I am a hero, and only for you I am a criminal and a thief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What did you say back to him?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: I said, Yes, I said that. But whoever conveyed that to you is an even bigger thief and criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was said after that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: After that I asked him this, Okay, if you're not a thief and a criminal then tell me what you are. I appreciate what you do. I know what you do. I understand what you do. And there will be a price to pay for that. What I'm interested in is my house, my property, and my status.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to ask him any particular question at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him a very concrete question. I told him this, I know that everybody is working for somebody. Tell me who your boss is. I want to make sure it's not Milosevic. He replied, Why are you asking me, you should know? And I said, No, I don't. And then he said, Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you ever personally met Jovica Stanisic or Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who is Brana Crncevic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Brana Crncevic was the president of the association of Serb immigrants. His office was in Nusiceva Street. For a while every time I came to Belgrade, I shared his office. And he asked me to raise funds for the association because there were already refugees and they had to be assisted. And I did that. I went to various companies. I did all sorts of fund-raising with various donors. And all I raised, all the assistance I raised was transferred to the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How often would you speak to him throughout June and July 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Every day. We shared the same office. He left around 11.00 every time, explaining that he had to go to President Milosevic. Every time he was about to leave, he told me what I'm supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "around 11.00 every time," you referring to how often a basis?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Every day. Every day when I was in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How often would it be that you were in the office?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: It depended on my other obligations, but it was very frequently, almost every morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where exactly was the office of Brana Crncevic located in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: The name of the street was Nusiceva. I can't remember the number. In any case, it's in the very centre of Belgrade between the big department store and casino hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where is this in relation to the office of Slobodan Milosevic at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Not far. President Milosevic's office was not even a kilometre away from there, also in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Crncevic in June or July 1991, in which he provided you with a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did this conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: In his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain what occurred in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: I said to Brana that on the following day I was headed for Erdut, although I was not allowed to go to Erdut, I was clear on that, there were a lot of warnings coming my way to that effect, but I wanted to see his reaction to my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: He told me to say to Arkan to call Sele on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you respond?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: I asked him to give me that in writing because I had so much to do and so much on my platter that I was afraid that I would not remember what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After you informed him that you would not remember this, what did Brana Crncevic do?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: He took a piece of paper that was on his desk and he wrote with a pencil something to the effect Arkan to call Sele on the phone. I don't know whether he signed the piece of paper or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did he write this piece of paper in your presence?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my presence. I was standing right by the -- his desk while he was jotting the words down, waiting for him to be over so I could take the piece of paper with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you personally familiar with the handwriting of Brana Crncevic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE SAVIC
utterances.text: If I saw it, I assume I would recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could Prosecution 65 ter 2882 please be placed before the witness. Could the Court Usher please enlarge the top half of this exhibit on the screen. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to read the following decision. It is the Chamber's determination pursuant to Rule 73 bis (C) of the Rules and a decision on Prosecution motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list. On the 5th of June, 2009, the Prosecution filed its amended and consolidated witness list pursuant to the Chamber's instruction of the 2nd of June, 2009. In its filing, the Prosecution requests the Chamber to re-evaluate the order of the 28th of April, 2008, which limited the Prosecution to present its case with 90 witnesses within 130 hours for examination-in-chief. The Prosecution argues that in contradiction with Rule 73 bis (C) the Pre-Trial Judge did not give the Prosecution a chance to be heard before determining the number of witnesses and time available for the Prosecution. The Prosecution requests the Chamber to allow for the presentation of ten additional witnesses within the allotted time-frame of 130 hours of examination-in-chief. The Chamber considers that for purposes of Rule 73 bis (C) the Prosecution has now been heard. The Chamber has considered the request by the Prosecution and has re-evaluated the assessment made by the Pre-Trial Judge on the 28th of April, 2008. Taking into account in particular the Prosecution's submission that the proposed ten additional witnesses would not affect the set time of 130 hours of examination-in-chief and having considered that six out of the additional ten witnesses are sought to be tendered pursuant to Rules 92 bis and -- it should read to Rule 92 bis and would, if called for cross-examination, due to their expected testimony only add a small amount of time for cross-examination to the overall length of the case, the Chamber grants the Prosecution's request to present evidence of an additional ten witnesses within the allotted time-frame. On the 6th of May, 2009, the Prosecution requested leave to add one witness to its Rule 65 ter witness list. The Stanisic Defence responded on the 20th of May, 2009, objecting to the motion. The Simatovic Defence did not respond. The Prosecution submits that the proposed witness would give additional evidence on the role of the Red Berets, which cannot be elicited from any of the crime base witnesses already on the witness list. It submits that it became aware of the witness's evidence in the summer of 2008 but waited with its motion until an official ICTY statement could be taken on the 15th of April, 2009. The Stanisic Defence submits that the Prosecution did not fulfil its obligation pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E)(ii)(d) of the Rules, in that it did not provide the Defence with a final list at least six weeks prior to the Pre-Trial Conference. The Stanisic Defence further submits that the Prosecution failed to advance a reasonable justification for this late addition. Pursuant to Rule 73 bis (F) of the Rules, the Chamber may grant any motion for an amendment to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list if satisfied that to do so is in the interests of justice. In this respect, the Chamber must balance the Prosecution's duty to present the available evidence to prove its case with the right of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial and the right to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of their defence. The Chamber will consider whether the proposed evidence is prima facie relevant and probative and whether the Prosecution has shown good cause why it did not seek to add the witness to its witness list at an earlier stage. Good cause may exist where the witness has only recently become available to give evidence or where the relevance of the evidence has only recently become apparent. The Chamber will further consider the burden placed on the Defence by the late addition of a witness to the Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber finds that the testimony of the proposed witness, given his unique position to provide certain evidence, is prima facie relevant and of probative value. As for good cause shown, the Chamber has learned from the submissions that the Defence was served with the statements and testimony of the proposed witness to Bosnian authorities in September and December 2008, respectively. Furthermore, according to the submissions from the Prosecution and the Stanisic Defence, the Prosecution notified the Defence on the 16th of January, 2009, of its intention to add the suggested witness to its witness list. Nevertheless, the Prosecution only succeeded in taking an official statement from the witness on the 15th of April, 2009. Considering the significant impact an interview with a possible witness might have on the decision on whether or not to request leave to amend the witness list, the Chamber finds that the Prosecution has shown good cause on why the request was not made earlier. The Chamber further considers that the Defence has been on notice for more than three months that the Prosecution would seek to add this witness to the witness list. Balancing the Prosecution's duty to present the available evidence to prove its case with the right of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial, the Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice to add the proposed witness to the Prosecution's witness list. On the 2nd of June, 2009, the Chamber stated that the Prosecution should further explain why the addition of the proposed witness would warrant an increase in the time of examination-in-chief available to it. This can be found at transcript pages 1382, 1397, and 1398. The Prosecution has not submitted any further specific arguments to that effect. The Chamber, therefore, decides that the Prosecution should present its case within the allotted time of 130 hours, even with the addition of the proposed witness. Accordingly, the Prosecution's motion is granted and the number of witnesses the Prosecution may call and the time available to it for presenting evidence is set to 101 witnesses and 130 hours respectively. This concludes the Chamber's determination pursuant to Rule 73 bis (C) of the Rules and its decision on the Prosecution motion for leave to amend the Rule 65 ter witness list. I first wanted to thank interpreters, transcriber, and all those, including security, assisting us for forgiveness at least, that's what I hope to get, to go seven minutes over the time set. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the - I have to look - the 7th of July, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.
